arXiv:1512.02475v2 [cond-mat.stat-mech] 24 Mar 2016

Low Autocorrelation Binary Sequences

Tom Packebusch    Stephan Mertens Email: mertens@ovgu.de Affiliation: Santa Fe Institute, 1399 Hyde Park Rd, Santa Fe, NM 87501, USA
Abstract

Binary sequences with minimal autocorrelations have applications in communication engineering, mathematics and computer science. In statistical physics they appear as groundstates of the Bernasconi model. Finding these sequences is a notoriously hard problem, that so far can be solved only by exhaustive search. We review recent algorithms and present a new algorithm that finds optimal sequences of length NN in time O⁡(N​ 1.73N)O(N\,1.73^{N}). We computed all optimal sequences for N≤66N\leq 66 and all optimal skewsymmetric sequences for N≤119N\leq 119.

1 Introduction

Consider a sequence S=(s1,…,sN)S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}) with si=±1s_{i}=\pm 1. The autocorrelations of SS are defined as

Ck​(S)=∑i=1N−ksi​si+kC_{k}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{N-k}s_{i}s_{i+k} (1)

for k=0,1,…,N−1k=0,1,\ldots,N-1, and the “energy” of SS is defined as the sum of the squares of all off-peak correlations,

E⁡(S)=∑k=1N−1Ck2​(S).E(S)=\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}C_{k}^{2}(S)\,. (2)

The low-autocorrelation binary sequence (LABS) problem is to find a sequence SS of given length NN that minimizes E⁡(S)E(S) or, equivalently, maximizes the merit factor

F⁡(S)=N22​E​(S).F(S)=\frac{N^{2}}{2E(S)}\,. (3)

The LABS problem arises in practical applications in communications engineering, where low autocorrelation sequences are used for example as modulation pulses in radar and sonar ranging [1, 2, 3]. A particularly exciting application is the interplanetary radar measurement of spacetime curvature [4].

In mathematics, the LABS problem appears in terms of the Littlewood problem [5, 6], the problem of constructing polynomials with coefficients ±1\pm 1 that are “flat” on the unit circle in the complex plane.

In statistical physics, E⁡(S)/NE(S)/N can be interpreted as the energy of NN interacting Ising spins si=±1s_{i}=\pm 1. This is the Bernasconi model [7]. It has long-range 4-spin interactions and is completely deterministic, i.e. there is no explicit or quenched disorder like in spin-glasses. Nevertheless the ground states are highly disordered – quasi by definition. This self-induced disorder resembles very much the situation in real glasses. In fact, the Bernasconi-model exhibits features of a glass transition like a jump in the specific heat and slow dynamics and aging [8]. A clever variation of the replica method allows an analytical treatment of the Bernasconi model in the high-temperature regime [9, 10]. For the low-temperature regime, analytical results are rare – especially the ground states are not known. Due to this connection to physics we refer to the sis_{i} as spins throughout the paper.

These examples illustrate the importance of the LABS problem in various fields. For more applications and the history of the problem we refer to existing surveys [11, 12]. In this contribution we focus on algorithms to solve the LABS problem. But before we discuss algorithms, we will give a brief survey on what is known about solutions.

2 What is known

The correlation CkC_{k} is the sum of N−kN-k terms ±1\pm 1, hence the value of |Ck||C_{k}| is bounded from below by

|Ck|≥bk=(N−k)mod2.|C_{k}|\geq b_{k}=(N-k)\bmod 2\,. (4)

A binary sequence with |Ck|=bk|C_{k}|=b_{k} is called a Barker sequence [13]. The merit factor of a Barker sequence is

FNBarker={Nfor N even,N2N−1for N odd.F_{N}^{\mathrm{Barker}}=\cases{N&for $N$ even,\\ \frac{N^{2}}{N-1}&for $N$ odd.} (5)

If it exists, a Barker sequence is a solution of the LABS problem. Barker sequences exist for N=2,3,4,5,7,11N=2,3,4,5,7,11 and 1313, but probably for no other values of NN. In fact it can be proven that there are no Barker sequences for odd values of N>13N>13 [14, 15]. For even values of NN, the existence of Barker sequences can be excluded for 4<N≤2​×​10304<N\leq\numprint{2e30} [16].

Let FNF_{N} denote the maximum merit factor for sequences of length NN. It is an open problem to prove (or disprove) that FNF_{N} is bounded. For Barker sequences, FN∝NF_{N}\propto N, and the same is true more generally for sequences such that |Ck|≤C⋆|C_{k}|\leq C^{\star} for some constant C⋆C^{\star} that does not depend on NN or kk. The common belief is that no such sequences exist and that FNF_{N} is bounded by some constant.

A non-rigorous argument for FNF_{N} being bounded was given by Golay [17]. Assuming that the correlations CkC_{k} are independent, he argued that asymptotically FN≲12.3248F_{N}\lesssim 12.3248, or more precisely, that

FN≲12.3248(8​π​N)32​N.F_{N}\lesssim\frac{12.3248}{(8\pi N)^{\frac{3}{2N}}}\,. (6)

There are some rigorous results for lower bounds on FNF_{N}. The mean value of 1/F1/F, taken over all binary sequences of length NN, is (N−1)/N(N-1)/N [18]. Hence we expect FN≥1F_{N}\geq 1. In fact one can explicetly construct sequences for all values of NN that have merit factors larger than 11. The current record is set by so called appended rotated Legendre sequences with an asymptotic merit factor of 6.342061​…6.342061\ldots [19, 20].

Beyond that, our knowledge about solutions of the LABS problem is based on computer searches. Figure 1 shows the best merit factors known for N<300N<300. For small values of NN, we can exhaustively search through all sequences to find the sequences with the maximum merit factor FNF_{N}. An evaluation of E⁡(S)E(S) from scratch takes time Θ⁡(N2)\Theta(N^{2}), but one can loop through all sequences sucht that any two successive sequences differ by exactly one spin, an arrangement known as Gray code [22]. The corresponding update of E⁡(S)E(S) takes only linear time, and the total time complexity of exhaustive enumeration is then given by Θ⁡(N​ 2N)\Theta(N\,2^{N}). In this paper we will discuss a class of exact enumeration algorithms with time complexity Θ⁡(N​bN)\Theta(N\,b^{N}) with b<2b<2 that we used to solve the LABS problem up to N≤66N\leq 66.

For larger values of NN exhaustive enumeration is not feasible and one has to resort to either partial enumerations or heuristic searches. In both cases one obtains sequences with large but not necessarily maximal merit factors.

Partial enumerations are exhaustive enumerations of a well defined subset of sequences. A particular promising subset is given by skewsymmetric sequences of odd length N=2​n−1N=2n-1. These sequences satisfy

sn+ℓ=(−1)ℓ​sn−ℓ(ℓ=1,…,n−1),s_{n+\ell}=(-1)^{\ell}s_{n-\ell}\qquad(\ell=1,\ldots,n-1)\,, (7)

which implies that Ck=0C_{k}=0 for all odd kk. The restriction to skewsymmetric sequences reduces the size of the search space from 2N2^{N} to 2N/22^{N/2}. Sequences with maximum merit factor are often, but not always skewsymmetric: from the 31 LABS problems for odd N≤65N\leq 65, 21 have skewsymmetric solutions (Section 4). For the other values of NN, skewsymmetric sequences provide lower bounds for FNF_{N}. We used our enumeration algorithm to compute the optimal skewsymmetric sequences for all N≤119N\leq 119.

Enumerative algorithms (complete or partial) are limited to small values of NN by the exponential size of the search space. Heuristic algorithms use some plausible rules to locate good sequences more quickly. Examples are simulated annealing, evolutionary algorithms, tabu search—the list of heuristic algorithms that have been applied to the LABS problem is much longer, see [23]. The state of the art are the solvers described in [21], which have found many of the merit factors shown in Figure 1. The figure shows a significant drop of the merit factors for N>200N>200. This is generally attributed to the fact that even sophisticated search heuristics fail for LABS problems of larger size. This hardness has earned the LABS problem a place in CSPLIB, a library of test problems for constraint solvers [24, problem 005].

3 Algorithm

According to the current state of knowledge, the only way to get exact solutions for the LABS problem is exhaustive search. With a search space that grows like 2N2^{N}, this approach is limited to rather small values of NN, however. The exponential complexity calls for a method to restrict the search to smaller subspaces without missing the exact solutions. This is where branch&bound comes in, a powerful and versatile method from combinatorial optimization [25]. All exact solutions of the LABS problem for N>32N>32 have been obtained with variations of a branch&bound algorithm proposed in [26] that reduces the size of the search space from 2N2^{N} to bNb^{N} with b<2b<2. In this section we review these algorithms and we present a new variant which has b=1.72b=1.72, the best value to date.

The idea of branch&bound is to solve a discrete optimization problem by breaking up its feasible set into successively smaller subsets (branch), calculating bounds on the objective function value over each subset, and using them to discard certain subsets from further consideration (bound) [25]. The procedure ends when each subset has either produced a feasible solution, or has been shown to contain no better solution than the one already in hand. The best solution found during this procedure is a global optimum.

The goal is of course to discard many subsets as early as possible during the branching process, i.e. to discard most of the feasible solutions before actually evaluating them. The success of this approach depends on the branching rule and very much on the quality of the bound, but it can be quite substantial.

For the LABS problem we specify a set of feasible solutions be fixing the mm leftmost and the mm rightmost spins of the sequence. The N−2​mN-2m centre spins are not specified, i. e. the set contains 2N−2​m2^{N-2m} feasible solutions. Given a feasible set specified by the 2​m2m outer elements, four smaller sets are created by fixing the elements sm+1s_{m+1} and sN−ms_{N-m} to ±1\pm 1 and mm is increased by 11. This is applied recursively until all elements have been fixed. This is the branching rule introduced by the original branch&bound algorithm [26], and it is shared by all later versions. It has the nice property that the long range correlations are fixed early in the recursion process. Specifically, if the mm left- and rightmost spins are fixed, all CkC_{k} for k≥N−mk\geq N-m are fixed. In addition, this branching rule supports the computation of lower bounds very well, as we will see below.

The branching process can be visualized as a tree in which nodes represent subsets. Each node has four children corresponding to the four possible ways to set the two spins in the (m+1)(m+1)th shell. The branch&bound algorithm traverses this tree and tries to exclude as many branches as possible by computing a bound on the energy that can be achieved in a branch. The number of nodes actually visited is a measure of quality for the bound.

3.1 Bounds

Bounds are usually obtained by replacing the original problem over a given subset with an easier (relaxed) problem such that the solution value of the latter bounds that of the former. A good relaxation is one that is easy and fast to solve and yields strong lower bounds. Most often these are conflicting goals.

An obvious relaxation of the LABS problem is given by the problem to minimize all values Ck2C_{k}^{2} independently. Hence we replace the original problem

Emin=minfree⁡(∑k=1N−1Ck2)E_{\mathrm{min}}=\min_{\mathrm{free}}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}C_{k}^{2}\right) (8)

by the relaxed version

Emin∗=∑k=1N−1minfree⁡(Ck2)=∑k=1N−1(minfree⁡(|Ck|))2≤Emin,E_{\mathrm{min}}^{*}=\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\min_{\mathrm{free}}(C_{k}^{2})=\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\left(\min_{\mathrm{free}}(|C_{k}|)\right)^{2}\leq E_{\mathrm{min}}\,, (9)

where “free” refers to the N−2​mN-2m center elements of ss that have not yet been assigned. All previous branch&bound approaches to LABS considered Emin∗E_{\mathrm{min}}^{*} to be too expensive to compute and replaced it by a weaker, but easily computable bound Eb≤Emin∗E_{b}\leq E_{\mathrm{min}}^{*} obtained from bounding minfree⁡|Ck|\min_{\mathrm{free}}|C_{k}| from below.

3.1.1 The original bound.

In the original algorithm [26] the bound EbE_{b} is computed by assigning (arbitrary) values to all free spins, thereby fixing the values for all correlations to Ck⋆C_{k}^{\star}. Since flipping a free spin can decrement |Ck||C_{k}| at most by 22, a lower bound for |Ck||C_{k}| is given by

minfree⁡|Ck|≥max⁡(bk,|Ck⋆|−2​f^k),\min_{\mathrm{free}}|C_{k}|\geq\max(b_{k},|C_{k}^{\star}|-2\hat{f}_{k})\,, (10)

where

f^k={0if k≥N−m,2​(N−m−k)if N/2≤k<N−m orN−2​motherwise\hat{f}_{k}=\cases{0&if $k\geq N-m$,\\ 2(N-m-k)&if $N/2\leq k<N-m$ or\\ N-2m&otherwise} (11)

denotes the number of free spins that appear in CkC_{k} and bkb_{k} is given by (4). The running time of this algorithm scales like O⁡(1.85N)O(1.85^{N}). A parallelized version of the algorithm was used to solve the LABS problem up to N=60N=60 [27].

3.1.2 The Prestwich bound.

The quality of the bound (10) depends on the values of Ck⋆C_{k}^{\star} and hence on the arbitrary values assigned to the free spins. In principle, these values should be chosen to maximize Ck⋆C_{k}^{\star}, but this requires the solution of another optimization problem for each bound. This can be avoided by considering free products instead of free spins: a product si​si+ks_{i}s_{i+k} is free if sis_{i} or si+ks_{i+k} is a free spin. Products si​si+ks_{i}s_{i+k} in which both spins are fixed ars called fixed. Let ck​(s)c_{k}(s) denote the sum of all fixed products that contribute to CkC_{k}. Note that ck=Ckc_{k}=C_{k} for k≥N−mk\geq N-m. Then

minfree⁡|Ck|≥max⁡(bk,|ck​(s)|−fk),\min_{\mathrm{free}}|C_{k}|\geq\max(b_{k},|c_{k}(s)|-f_{k})\,, (12)

where

fk=(N−k)−2​max⁡(m−k,0)−max⁡(k−N+2​m,0)f_{k}=(N-k)-2\max(m-k,0)-\max(k-N+2m,0) (13)

denotes the number of free products in CkC_{k}, and bkb_{k} is given by (4). The reasoning behind (12) is that the sum ckc_{k} of fixed products may be offset by the sum of free products, which is no greater than fkf_{k}. If |ck​(s)|>fk|c_{k}(s)|>f_{k} then |ck​(s)|−fk|c_{k}(s)|-f_{k} is a lower bound for |Ck||C_{k}|. If |ck​(s)|≤fk|c_{k}(s)|\leq f_{k}, this bound is useless and we have to resort to the trivial lower bound |Ck​(s)|≥bk|C_{k}(s)|\geq b_{k}. The bound (12) was used by Prestwich to prune parts of the search space in a local search algorithm for the LABS problem [28].

For his recent branch&bound algorithm for LABS, Prestwich [29] improved that bound by taking into account some of the interactions between fixed and free spins. Suppose that sis_{i} is a free spin while si−ks_{i-k} and si+ks_{i+k} are fixed. If si−k≠si+ks_{i-k}\neq s_{i+k}, the contributions

si−k​si+si​si+k=si​(si−k+si+k)s_{i-k}s_{i}+s_{i}s_{i+k}=s_{i}(s_{i-k}+s_{i+k}) (14)

of sis_{i} to CkC_{k} are zero, no matter what the value of sis_{i} is. For each such cancellation, the number fkf_{k} in (12) can be decreased by two. For si−k=si+ks_{i-k}=s_{i+k}, the contribution of the term (14) is ±2\pm 2, a situation referred to as reinforcement by Prestwich. Now, if all free contributions to CkC_{k} are either cancellations or reinforcements, then fkf_{k} must be even. If the sum of the fixed contributions ckc_{k} is also even and ckmod4≠fkmod4c_{k}\bmod 4\neq f_{k}\bmod 4, we can set bk=2b_{k}=2 in (12). With this bound, Prestwich reports a running time that scales like O⁡(1.80N)O(1.80^{N}). Since Prestwich didn’t parallelize his algorithm, this estimate was based on enumerations only up to N≤44N\leq 44.

3.1.3 The Wiggenbrock bound.

A different bound was used by Wiggenbrock in his branch&bound algorithm [30]. Flipping a spin changes the sum Ck+CN−kC_{k}+C_{N-k} by ±4\pm 4 because every spin occurs twice in that sum. Taking the all +1+1 configuration as a reference, we get

(N−CN−k)≡Ck(mod4).(N-C_{N-k})\equiv C_{k}\pmod{4}\,. (15)

For k≥N−mk\geq N-m, the CkC_{k} are completely fixed. For other values of kk, the correlations can be bounded by

|Ck|≥{|(N−CN−k)mod4|if k≤m,bkif m<k<N−m,|C_{k}|\geq\cases{|(N-C_{N-k})\bmod 4|&if $k\leq m$,\\ b_{k}&if $m<k<N-m$,} (16)

where we assumed the residue system {−1,0,1,2}\{-1,0,1,2\} for the mod 4 operation.

The Wiggenbrock bound seems to be weak since it bounds |Ck||C_{k}| by small numbers 0,1,20,1,2 only. Yet it is surprisingly efficient: Wiggenbrock reported a running time of O⁡(1.79N)O(1.79^{N}), slightly better than the scaling of Prestwich’s bound. Using a parallelized implementation and running it on 18 GPUs, Wiggenbrock solved the LABS problem for N≤64N\leq 64 [30].

3.1.4 The combined bound.

High up in the search tree, where mm is small, the contributions of the free products overcompensate the fixed contributions and the Prestwich bound (12) reduces to bkb_{k}. The Wiggenbrock bound (16) provides a better bound in exactly these situations. The fact that it yields such a good running time indicates that even this weak bound is efficient because it applies high up in the search tree: a branch, that can be pruned at this level, is usually very large. The Prestwich bound with the free products applies for larger values of mm, on the other hand. An obvious idea is to combine these complimentary bounds and use

|Ck|≥{max⁡(|(N−CN−k)mod4|,|ck​(s)|−fk)if k≤m,max⁡(bk,|ck​(s)|−fk)if m<k<N−m,|C_{k}|\geq\cases{\max\big(|(N-C_{N-k})\bmod 4|,|c_{k}(s)|-f_{k}\big)&if $k\leq m$,\\ \max(b_{k},|c_{k}(s)|-f_{k})&if $m<k<N-m$,} (17)

as a bound.

When we measure the number of recursive calls (i.e. the number of nodes visited in the search tree) and the CPU time per call (Figure 2), we find that the running time of the branch&bound algorithm with the combined bound (17) scales like Θ⁡(N​1.729N)\Theta(N1.729^{N}).

3.1.5 The tight bound.

So far, all bounds are lower bounds for min⁡|Ck|\min|C_{k}| that yield only a lower bound for Emin∗E_{\mathrm{min}}^{*}, which already is a lower bound for EminE_{\mathrm{min}}. We will now show that min⁡|Ck|\min|C_{k}| and hence Emin∗E_{\mathrm{min}}^{*} can be computed exactly, thereby avoiding the “second relaxation” to EbE_{b} and providing the best lower bound possible from the Ansatz (9). We write CkC_{k} as

Ck=ck+uk,C_{k}=c_{k}+u_{k}\,, (18)

where ckc_{k} is the sum of all fixed terms si​si+ks_{i}s_{i+k} (as above) and uku_{k} sums up all terms in which at least one spin is free. Let

gk={4if k≤m,2otherwise.g_{k}=\cases{4&if $k\leq m$,\\ 2&otherwise.} (19)

We will show below that there exist easy to compute integers UkminU_{k}^{\mathrm{min}} and UkmaxU_{k}^{\mathrm{max}} such that the free contribution uku_{k} can take on all values in

{Ukmin,Ukmin+gk,Ukmin+2​gk,…,Ukmax−gk,Ukmax}\{U_{k}^{\mathrm{min}},U_{k}^{\mathrm{min}}+g_{k},U_{k}^{\mathrm{min}}+2g_{k},\ldots,U_{k}^{\mathrm{max}}-g_{k},U_{k}^{\mathrm{max}}\} (20)

All we need to know are the values of ckc_{k}, UkminU_{k}^{\mathrm{min}} and UkmaxU_{k}^{\mathrm{max}} to compute

min⁡|Ck|={ck+Ukminif −ck≤Ukmin,ck+Ukmaxif −ck≥Ukmax,|(−ck−Ukmin)modgk|otherwise,\min|C_{k}|=\cases{c_{k}+U_{k}^{\mathrm{min}}&if $-c_{k}\leq U_{k}^{\mathrm{min}}$,\\ c_{k}+U_{k}^{\mathrm{max}}&if $-c_{k}\geq U_{k}^{\mathrm{max}}$,\\ |(-c_{k}-U_{k}^{\mathrm{min}})\bmod g_{k}|&otherwise,} (21)

and then Emin∗=∑k(min⁡|Ck|)2E_{\mathrm{min}}^{*}=\sum_{k}(\min|C_{k}|)^{2}.

To prove (19) and (20), we rearrange the sum (1) for CkC_{k} a little bit. For C3C_{3} and N=12N=12, for example, we can write

C3\displaystyle C_{3} =\displaystyle= s1​s4+s1​s4+s1​s4+s1​s4+s1​s4+s1​s4+s1​s4+s1​s4+s1​s4\displaystyle s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}+s_{1}s_{4}
=\displaystyle= (s1​s4+s4​s7+s7​s10)+(s2​s5+s5​s8+s8​s11)+(s3​s6+s6​s9+s9​s12).\displaystyle(s_{1}s_{4}+s_{4}s_{7}+s_{7}s_{10})+(s_{2}s_{5}+s_{5}s_{8}+s_{8}s_{11})+(s_{3}s_{6}+s_{6}s_{9}+s_{9}s_{12})\,.

We call every sum in parentheses a chain. For general values of kk and NN we write

Ck=∑j=1k∑q=1⌊N−jk⌋sj+(q−1)​k​sj+q​k.C_{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{q=1}^{\lfloor\frac{N-j}{k}\rfloor}s_{j+(q-1)k}s_{j+qk}\,. (22)

The chains are the sums over qq. For k<N−mk<N-m, each chain contains a subchain of free terms

sa​sa+k+sa+k​sa+2​k+⋯+sb−k​sbs_{a}s_{a+k}+s_{a+k}s_{a+2k}+\cdots+s_{b-k}s_{b}\, (23)

where only the spins sas_{a} and sbs_{b} may be fixed. We refer to these subchains as free chains. The sum of all free chains equals uku_{k}.

Let us first prove the “granularity” (19). If both spins sas_{a} and sbs_{b} are fixed, then every free spin appears exactly in two terms, and flipping any free spin changes the sum (23) by 00 or ±4\pm 4. If either sas_{a} or sbs_{b} (or both) are free, then flipping this spin changes the sum (23) by ±2\pm 2. Hence the granularity gkg_{k} is 44 if and only if all contributing free chains have both sas_{a} and sbs_{b} fixed, and 22 otherwise.

Now sas_{a} can be free and the leftmost member of a free chain if and only if a>ma>m and if it has no left partner, i.e. if a−k≤0a-k\leq 0. Together, both conditions imply k>mk>m. Hence by argumentum e contrario, k≤mk\leq m implies that sas_{a} is fixed and, by similar reasoning, also that that sbs_{b} is fixed. This proves that gk=4g_{k}=4 for k≤mk\leq m.

If k>mk>m, we only need to find a single free chain that starts with a free spin. Consider the spin sm+1s_{m+1}: It is free and it has no left neighbor. Hence it is the leftmost spin of a free chain that contributes to uku_{k}. Therefore gk=2g_{k}=2 for k>mk>m. Note that for k>mk>m there can be free chains with both sas_{a} and sbs_{b} fixed. All we have proven is that for k>mk>m this can’t happen for all free chains.

Now we will prove (20). Let nn denote the number of terms sj​sj+ks_{j}s_{j+k} in a free chain (23), and let uu denote its value. If sas_{a} or sbs_{b} (or both) are free, then uu can take on all values between −n-n and nn with granularity 22:

u∈[−n,−n+2,…,n−2,n](sa or sb free).u\in[-n,-n+2,\ldots,n-2,n]\qquad\mbox{($s_{a}$ or $s_{b}$ free).} (24)

If both spins sas_{a} and sbs_{b} are fixed, the granularity is 44 and the range of values varies with sas_{a}, sbs_{b} and the parity of nn according to

u∈{[−n,…,n]if sa=sb and n even,if sa=sb and n odd,if sa≠sb and n even,if sa≠sb and n odd.u\in\cases{[-n,\ldots,n]&if $s_{a}=s_{b}$ and $n$ even,\\[0.0pt] &if $s_{a}=s_{b}$ and $n$ odd,\\[0.0pt] &if $s_{a}\neq s_{b}$ and $n$ even,\\[0.0pt] &if $s_{a}\neq s_{b}$ and $n$ odd.} (25)

This can be proven by induction over nn. For nn odd, the base case is n=3n=3, i.e.

u=sa​sa+k+sa+k​sb−k+sb−k​sb.u=s_{a}s_{a+k}+s_{a+k}s_{b-k}+s_{b-k}s_{b}\,.

For sa≠sbs_{a}\neq s_{b}, the center term is −1-1 and umax=1u_{\mathrm{max}}=1. The value of uu is minimized by setting sa+k=−sas_{a+k}=-s_{a} and sb−k=−sbs_{b-k}=-s_{b}. If sa=sbs_{a}=s_{b}, the center term is 11 and umin=−1u_{\mathrm{min}}=-1. If sa≠sbs_{a}\neq s_{b}, the center term is −1-1 and umin=−3u_{\mathrm{min}}=-3. Now let us assume that (25) holds for some odd n≥3n\geq 3 and consider a free chain

u=sa​sa+k+sa+k​sa+2​k+⋯+sb−2​k​sb−k+sb−k​sbu=s_{a}s_{a+k}+s_{a+k}s_{a+2k}+\cdots+s_{b-2k}s_{b-k}+s_{b-k}s_{b}

with n+2n+2 terms. To maximize uu, we set sa+k=sas_{a+k}=s_{a} and sb−k=sbs_{b-k}=s_{b}, and the remaining free chain has nn terms. Applying (25), we get umax=n+2u_{\mathrm{max}}=n+2 if sa=sbs_{a}=s_{b} and umax=nu_{\mathrm{max}}=n if sa≠sbs_{a}\neq s_{b}. The induction step for uminu_{\mathrm{min}} is obvious.

Since the proof for even nn is very similar, it is omitted here. We only mention that the base case (n=2n=2) corresponds to the “cancellation” and “reinforcement” used by Prestwich to improve the bound (12).

Now (24) and (25) tell us how to compute uminu_{\mathrm{min}} and umaxu_{\mathrm{max}} for each individual free chain. The corresponding values UkminU_{k}^{\mathrm{min}} and UkmaxU_{k}^{\mathrm{max}} are obtained by summing over all free chains that contribute to uku_{k}.

Every branch of the search tree that can be pruned according to the combined bound (17) (or any other relaxation of (9)) is also pruned by the tight bound (21), but the tight bound allows us to prune additional branches. Hence the number of recursive calls with the tight bound can not be larger than the number of calls with any other bound based on (9). What we observe is that for N≤66N\leq 66 the number of calls for the tight bound is in fact strictly smaller than that for the combined bound. A numerical fit to the existing data yields a scaling of Θ⁡(1.727N)\Theta(1.727^{N}) for the tight bound, compared to Θ⁡(1.729N)\Theta(1.729^{N}) for the combined bound, see Figure 2. This difference is too small to tell whether the tight bound actually provides an exponential speedup or not. In fact, if one looks at the ratio of the number of calls for the combined bound divided by the number of calls for the tight bound, one observes that the speedup factor grows linearly with NN, not exponentially (Figure 3). Since the time per call scales linearly for both bounds (Figure 2 bottom), a reduction of the number of calls that grows with NN implies that the tight bound will asymptotically outperform the combined bound.

For the values of NN considered in this paper, however, the absolute computational costs per call matter. And here the simpler combined bound (17) is faster, see Figure 2 (bottom). If we extrapolate the number of calls and the time per call to N=66N=66, we get a running time of roughly 12600 CPU days for the combined bound but 14300 CPU days for the tight bound. This is why we used the weaker combined bound for all the new solutions (exact and skewsymmetric) reported in this paper. Note that the time per call depends considerably on the implementation. It might well be possible to implement the tight bound such that it outperforms the combined bound already for the values of NN considered here. In any case, the measured running times illustrate that we need to parallelize the computation if we don’t want to wait 35 years for the N=66N=66 LABS solution.

3.2 Symmetry and Parallelization

The correlations CkC_{k} (1) are unchanged when the sequence is complemented or reversed. When alternate elements of the sequence are complemented, the even-indexed correlations are not affected, the odd-indexed correlations only change sign. Hence, with the exception of a small number of symmetric sequences, the 2N2^{N} sequences will come in classes of eight which are equivalent. The total number of nonequivalent sequences is slightly larger than 2N−32^{N-3}.

The mm left- and mm rightmost elements of the sequence can be used to parameterize the symmetry classes. The total number c⁡(m)c(m) of symmetry classes that can be distinguished by mm left- and mm right-border elements reads

c⁡(m)=22​m−3+2m−2+(Nmod2).c(m)=2^{2m-3}+2^{m-2+(N\bmod 2)}\,. (26)

We derive this formula in A, where we also describe how to compute the values of the 2​m2m boundary spins that represent each symmetry class.

The symmetry classes can be enumerated independently, which allows us to parallelize the computation. For our largest system (N=66N=66) we used c⁡(m=10)=131 328c(m=10)=\numprint{131328} symmetry classes that we searched in parallel on various computers with number of computing cores ranging from 8 to 5 700. In principle, the branch&bound algorithm requires some communication between the parallel tasks since every task should know the lowest energy found so far by other tasks to compare it to the bound. We avoid this communication completely by using a static value for this reference energy: the lowest energy found by heuristic searches. In all cases we considered, this value turned out to be the true minimum energy.

4 Results and Conclusions

We have used the branch&bound algorithm with the combined bound to compute all sequences with maximum merit factor for N≤66N\leq 66, see Tables 1 and 2. The previous record was N≤64N\leq 64, obtained with the Wiggenbrock bound (16) and using 18 GPUs [30]. For the perfomance measurements for 40≤N≤6440\leq N\leq 64 shown in Figure 2 we have used a Linux cluster with a collection of Intel® Xeon® CPUs: 10×10\times E5-2630 (at 2.30 Ghz), 10×10\times E5-2630 v2 (at 2.60 Ghz) and 2×2\times E5-1620 (at 3.60 Ghz) with a total of 248 (virtual) cores. On this machine, the computation for N=64N=64 took about a week (wallclock time). As one can see in Figure 2, the solution of N=63N=63 and N=64N=64 involves a surprisingly low number of calls and took therefore less time than actually expected.

Note that with our algorithm systems of size N≤43N\leq 43 can be solved in less than an hour on a laptop.

For N=65N=65 and N=66N=66 we used a variety of computing machinery that makes an accurate determination of “single CPU time” impossible. For N=65N=65 and 66, the equivalent wallclock time on our benchmark cluster is roughly 32 and 55 days.

Tables 1 and 2 show all sequences (except those related by symmetries) with maximum merit factors up to N=66N=66 in run-length encoding, i.e. the digits specify the length of runs of equal spins. We use a=10a=10, b=11b=11 etc. for runs of spins that are longer than 99.

We have used our branch&bound algorithm also to find all skewsymmetric sequences with maximum merit factor up to N=119N=119. The previous record was N≤89N\leq 89 [29]. Table 3 shows the skewsymmetric sequences with maximum merit factor as far as they are not listed in Tables 1 and 2. Skewsymmetric merit factors marked with ⋆\star are known to be not maximal. We know this either from exhaustive enumerations (for N≤65N\leq 65) or from heuristic searches that have yielded non skewsymmetric sequences with larger merit factors.

Figure 4 shows the ratio of the maximum merit factors of skewsymmetric and general sequences for N≤119N\leq 119. In 20 out of 58 cases the skewsymmetric subset does not contain a maximum merit factor sequence. Note that the values of FNF_{N} for N>66N>66 are from heuristic searches, but we believe that these values are the true maximum merit factors. But strictly speaking, the gray symbols in Figure 4 are only upper bounds for the ratio FNskew/FNF_{N}^{\mathrm{skew}}/F_{N}. The available data seems to indicate that roughly two thirds of all odd values of NN have skewsymmetric maximum merit factor sequences. Figure 4 also suggests that

lim infN→∞FNskewFN=1.\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{F_{N}^{\mathrm{skew}}}{F_{N}}=1\,. (27)

We think that the branch&bound approach based on the relaxation (9) can be used to solve the LABS problem for N>66N>66 by devoting more compute cores and more CPU time. Improving the implementation to reduce the constant factor in the Θ⁡(N​bN)\Theta(N\,b^{N}) scaling can also help. Solving systems significantly larger than N=66N=66, however, requires a stronger bound than (9), i.e., a bound that takes into account the fact that the CkC_{k} are not independent. Or a completely new approach other than branch&bound.

Appendix A Symmetry

To find the exact number of symmetry classes in the LABS problem we need some group theory. The operators RR (reverse), CC (complement) and AA (alternate complement) act on the sequences, leaving the energy invariant. Together with the identity operator II these operators generate a group GG of order 88. The structure of GG depends on NN being odd or even.

For NN even, G=GeG=G_{e} is non-abelian and isomorphic to the dihedral group D4D_{4}, the symmetry group of a square plate, generated by a 90 degree rotation and a flip. The elements of GeG_{e} are {I,R,C,A,R​A,A​R,R​C,A​C}\{I,R,C,A,RA,AR,RC,AC\}. The group elements act on a sequence ss. Let

G⁡(s):={g⁡(s):g∈G}G(s):=\{g(s):g\in G\} (28)

denote the orbit of ss, i.e. the set of all spin sequences that can be generated from ss by application of the group elements. The length of the orbit is |G⁡(s)||G(s)|. The orbits partition the set of all spin sequences in the symmetry classes we want to count. If all orbits were of length 88, we would have 2N−32^{N-3} symmetry classes. Unfortunately there are orbits of smaller length, to wit

G(++++)={++++,−−−−,−+−+,+−+−}.G(++++)=\{++++,----,-+-+,+-+-\}.

The true number cc of orbits is given by Burnside’s Lemma,

c=1|G|​∑g∈G|Fix⁡(g)|,c=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\mathrm{Fix}(g)|\,, (29)

where Fix⁡(g)={s:g⁡(s)=s}\mathrm{Fix}(g)=\{s:g(s)=s\} denotes the set of all sequences ss that are fixed points of gg. The group elements AA, CC, A​RAR, R​ARA and A​CAC can’t fix a sequence, but RR and R​CRC can. Sequences with sj=sN+1−js_{j}=s_{N+1-j} are fixed by RR, sequences with sj=−sN+1−js_{j}=-s_{N+1-j} are fixed by R​CRC, and there are 2N/22^{N/2} sequences of each type. Hence

cN​even=18​(|Fix⁡(I)|+|Fix⁡(R)|+|Fix⁡(R​C)|)=2N−3+2N/2−2.c_{N\mathrm{even}}=\frac{1}{8}\left(|\mathrm{Fix}(I)|+|\mathrm{Fix}(R)|+|\mathrm{Fix}(RC)|\right)=2^{N-3}+2^{N/2-2}. (30)

For NN odd, the group G=GoG=G_{o} is again of order 88, but this time it is abelian. Group elements are Go={I,R,C,A,R​C,R​A,C​A,R​C​A}G_{o}=\{I,R,C,A,RC,RA,CA,RCA\}, and g2=Ig^{2}=I for all g∈Gog\in G_{o}. GoG_{o} is isomorphic to the reflection-symmetry group of the cube. If (N−1)/2(N-1)/2 is odd, only RR, R​ARA and II have fixed points. Sequences that are fixed by RR have sj=sN+1−js_{j}=s_{N+1-j} with arbitrary center spin s(N+1)/2s_{(N+1)/2}. There are 2⋅2(N−1)/22\cdot 2^{(N-1)/2} such sequences. The same number of sequences are fixed by R​ARA. Hence

cN​odd=18​(|Fix⁡(I)|+|Fix⁡(R)|+|Fix⁡(R​A)|)=2N−3+2(N−1)/2−1.c_{N\mathrm{odd}}=\frac{1}{8}\left(|\mathrm{Fix}(I)|+|\mathrm{Fix}(R)|+|\mathrm{Fix}(RA)|\right)=2^{N-3}+2^{(N-1)/2-1}. (31)

If (N−1)/2(N-1)/2 is even, only II, RR and R​C​ARCA have fixed points, and their numbers are the same as in (31). Combining (30) and (31) provides us with

cN=2N−3+2(N−1)/2−2+(Nmod2).c_{N}=2^{N-3}+2^{(N-1)/2-2+(N\bmod 2)}\,. (32)

This is the total number of symmetry classes if we consider all elements of the sequence. If we only consider the mm leftmost and mm rightmost elements, the arguments are similar. For NN even, the symmetry group Ge={I,R,C,A,R​A,A​R,R​C,A​C}G_{e}=\{I,R,C,A,RA,AR,RC,AC\} acts only on the 2​m2m elements, and only II, RR and R​CRC have fixed points. Hence

c⁡(m)=22​m−3+2m−2N even.c(m)=2^{2m-3}+2^{m-2}\qquad\mbox{$N$ even.} (33)

For NN odd, the symmetry group is again Go={I,R,C,A,R​C,R​A,C​A,R​C​A}G_{o}=\{I,R,C,A,RC,RA,CA,RCA\}, but this time II, RR, R​CRC, R​ARA and R​C​ARCA have fixed points:

c⁡(m)=22​m−3+2m−1N odd.c(m)=2^{2m-3}+2^{m-1}\qquad\mbox{$N$ odd.} (34)

Combining (33) and (34) provides us with (26).

The c⁡(m)c(m) symmetry classes can be uniquely parameterized by the values of the 2​m2m boundary spins. Consider the list of all 22​m2^{2m} possible configurations of the boundary spins. For each such configuration compute G​(s)=Ge​(s)G(s)=G_{e}(s) (for NN even) or G​(s)=Go​(s)G(s)=G_{o}(s) (for NN odd). If ss is not the lexicographically smallest element in G⁡(s)G(s), remove it from the list. The remaining elements are a unique representation of the symmetry classes.
